subject: Surgery
summary: The ICU supports patients with failing organs after surgery or trauma. In low‑resource African hospitals clinicians must prioritize rapid assessment, use limited investigations wisely, and apply core supportive measures.

sections.p: An Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is a specialised ward providing continuous monitoring and organ‑support for patients with life‑threatening physiological derangement after surgery, trauma or severe medical illness.
b: 1:1 nursing ratio or highest feasible staffing
Continuous ECG, pulse oximetry, non‑invasive BP, and capnography when possible

sections.p: Severity is graded by organ‑failure scores; the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) is most widely used.
b: SOFA ≥2 indicates early organ dysfunction; ≥10 predicts >80% mortality
In low‑resource settings, a simplified bedside SOFA (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, hepatic, neurologic, coagulation) guides escalation

sections.p: Common surgical ICU admissions in East Africa include:
b: Severe sepsis from intra‑abdominal infection or wound sepsis
Traumatic hemorrhage with hypovolemic shock
Post‑operative respiratory failure (aspiration, pneumonia, ARDS)
Cardiogenic shock after cardiac surgery or massive myocardial infarction
Malaria‑related severe anemia or cerebral malaria requiring ventilation

sections.p: Patients arrive with altered mental status, tachypnoea, hypotension, oliguria, or refractory hypoxaemia.
b: Cold, clammy skin and delayed capillary refill suggest shock
Decreased urine <0.5 mL/kg/h signals renal hypoperfusion
PaO₂/FiO₂ <300 indicates acute lung injury; <200 defines ARDS

t.b: Answers acid‑base status and oxygenation; a PaO₂/FiO₂ <200 confirms ARDS

t.a: Full blood count & malaria rapid test
t.b: Detects anemia, leukocytosis, malaria; treat malaria promptly if positive
Reflects tissue hypoperfusion; >2 mmol/L signals ongoing shock
Guides fluid and drug dosing; rising creatinine >2 mg/dL suggests AKI
Identifies infiltrates, pneumothorax, pulmonary oedema; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs and ultrasound
Answers volume status, pleural effusion, cardiac contractility; if no machine, use bedside clinical assessment

sections.p: Complications develop rapidly and require immediate action.
b: Uncontrolled hemorrhage → drop in systolic BP >20 mmHg or loss of pulse pressure
Ventilator‑associated pneumonia – new fever, purulent sputum, infiltrate after >48 h
Acute kidney injury – urine <0.3 mL/kg/h for >6 h
Septic shock – lactate >4 mmol/L despite fluids

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide organ support using resources available.
b: Airway: head‑tilt‑chin‑lift; if unconscious, insert a cuffed endotracheal tube; use bag‑valve‑mask if no ventilator
Breathing: give oxygen 10‑15 L/min via mask; consider CPAP or BiPAP if ventilator unavailable
Circulation: 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus; if shock persists, start norepinephrine infusion (avoid dopamine in tachyarrhythmia)
Infection: broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) within 1 h; add antimalarial if test positive
Sedation/analgesia: low‑dose morphine or fentanyl; avoid high‑dose haloperidol in septic patients due to QT prolongation
Nutrition: start enteral feeding within 24 h if gut functional; use locally available formulas

sections.p: After stabilisation, plan step‑down to high‑dependency or ward and address preventable factors.
b: Early mobilisation and physiotherapy to prevent deconditioning
Strict aseptic technique for lines to reduce catheter infections
Malaria prophylaxis and insect‑net distribution for at‑risk patients
Vaccination against hepatitis B for surgical staff and patients
High‑dependency unit (HDU) – lower nurse‑patient ratio, less invasive support
Neonatal ICU – cares for newborns, not adult surgical patients

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, some values may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal lactate early in malaria may mask impending shock; repeat testing
Chest X‑ray may miss early ARDS; rely on oxygenation index
Creatinine may be low in malnourished patients despite renal injury

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of pulse or cardiac arrest
Unresponsive patient with GCS ≤8 despite airway measures
Severe refractory hypotension after two fluid boluses

faq.q: What is the first action for a patient with suspected airway obstruction in the ICU?
faq.a: Secure the airway immediately with head‑tilt‑chin‑lift and, if needed, rapid sequence intubation.

faq.q: Why avoid dopamine in septic shock when norepinephrine is available?
faq.a: Dopamine increases arrhythmia risk and has variable α/β effects; norepinephrine provides reliable vasoconstriction.

faq.q: How can you estimate fluid responsiveness without a monitor?
faq.a: Assess passive leg raise or look for improvement in capillary refill and urine output after a small fluid bolus.

exam: A 45‑year‑old male post‑laparotomy becomes tachypnoeic, SpO₂ 85% on 6 L O₂, and has bilateral crackles – what is your next step and why? — Assess for ARDS, start CPAP or mechanical ventilation, and give lung‑protective strategy because hypoxaemia threatens organ perfusion.

You receive a septic patient with a lactate of 3.5 mmol/L after 30 mL/kg fluids – what does this indicate and what should you do? — Persistent hyperlactataemia signals ongoing shock; start norepinephrine infusion and reassess source control.

A trauma patient in the ICU shows urine output 0.2 mL/kg/h despite adequate fluids – what is the likely problem and management? — Acute kidney injury from renal hypoperfusion; consider diuretics only after optimizing perfusion, monitor electrolytes, and plan renal replacement if no improvement.
Why is routine prophylactic antacid therapy discouraged in the surgical ICU? — It raises risk of ventilator‑associated pneumonia and Clostridioides difficile without clear benefit.
A patient on ceftriaxone develops a rash and eosinophilia – what is the likely diagnosis and next step? — Drug‑induced hypersensitivity; stop ceftriaxone and switch to a non‑β‑lactam antibiotic.

Explain how you would differentiate cardiogenic shock from hypovolemic shock without invasive monitoring. — Look for warm, flushed skin and high CVP in cardiogenic shock versus cold, clammy skin, low CVP, and brisk pulse pressure in hypovolemia; use bedside ultrasound for cardiac contractility.
What are the key components of nutrition support in the first 48 h of ICU admission? — Early enteral feeding, glucose control <180 mg/dL, protein 1.2‑1.5 g/kg/day, and electrolyte monitoring.

When is it appropriate to transfer a patient from ICU to a high‑dependency unit? — When organ support is stable (e.g., off vasopressors, on low‑flow oxygen, urine >0.5 mL/kg/h) and the patient can be safely monitored with a lower nurse‑patient ratio.
